oneLine: Draw the five core charts with Matplotlib and Seaborn, know which call makes which chart, and read what each one shows.

know.cue: Which Seaborn function draws each core chart?
know.fact: `sns.histplot` (histogram), `sns.boxplot` (box plot), `sns.scatterplot` (scatter), `sns.lineplot` (line) and `sns.heatmap` (heatmap, often of `df.corr()`).
know.why: Items describe a chart and ask for the call.

know.cue: How do Matplotlib's two interfaces differ?
know.fact: The pyplot style (`plt.plot`, `plt.title`) acts on the current figure; the object-oriented style (`fig, ax = plt.subplots()`, `ax.plot`, `ax.set_title`) calls methods on explicit Axes.
know.why: Code items mix the two and ask which line is valid.

know.cue: What does `plt.subplots(2, 2)` return?
know.fact: A figure and a 2 × 2 array of Axes, indexed as `axes[row, col]`; pass `ax=axes[r, c]` to Seaborn functions to draw on one of them.
know.why: Dashboard-style items use subplot grids.

know.cue: How do `sns.barplot` and `sns.countplot` differ?
know.fact: `barplot` shows the mean of a numeric column per category (with an error bar); `countplot` shows how many rows fall in each category.
know.why: A frequent distractor pair.

know.cue: How do you save a figure?
know.fact: `fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")`, called before `plt.show()`, which may clear the figure.
know.why: Items ask why a saved file is blank.

traps.answer: It colours the marks by a categorical column, adding a legend for the groups.
Not when x values repeat: it averages them and draws a confidence band by default.

oneLine: Choose the chart from the question: trends → line, comparisons → bar, distributions → histogram or box plot, relationships → scatter, many correlations → heatmap.

know.cue: Which chart shows a trend over time?
know.fact: A line chart: time on the x-axis, the value on the y-axis.
know.why: The most common chart-choice item.

know.cue: Which chart compares values across categories?
know.fact: A bar chart, ideally sorted, horizontal for long labels, with the value axis starting at zero.
know.why: Pie charts are the usual distractor.

know.cue: Which charts show a single variable's distribution?
know.fact: A histogram (shape, skew, modality) or a box plot (median, IQR, outliers); side-by-side box plots compare groups.
know.why: "Compare salary spread across departments" → box plots.

know.cue: When is a pie chart acceptable?
know.fact: Only for parts of a whole with two to five slices; angles are hard to compare, so bar charts are usually clearer.
know.why: Items ask what's wrong with a 12-slice pie.

know.cue: How do truncated axes and 3D effects mislead?
know.fact: A bar chart whose axis doesn't start at zero exaggerates differences, and 3D perspective distorts sizes.
know.why: Items show a misleading chart and ask for the fix.

traps.cue: Should you draw a line chart for unordered categories such as product names?
traps.answer: No. A line implies order and continuity; use a bar chart.

traps.cue: What does a box plot hide?
traps.answer: Multiple peaks (bimodality) and the sample size. A histogram or violin plot shows the shape.

oneLine: Title with the takeaway, label axes with units, annotate what matters, and control legends, colours and ranges precisely.

know.cue: Which calls set the title and axis labels?
know.fact: `ax.set_title`, `ax.set_xlabel` and `ax.set_ylabel` in the object-oriented style, or `plt.title`, `plt.xlabel` and `plt.ylabel` in pyplot style.
know.why: Direct recall items.

know.cue: How do you control a legend's position, font size and background?
know.fact: Give each series a `label=`, then call `ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9, facecolor="white", framealpha=1)`; `bbox_to_anchor` moves it outside the axes.
know.why: The syllabus names legend position, font size and background colour.

know.cue: How do you point out a specific data point?
know.fact: `ax.annotate("text", xy=(x, y), xytext=(tx, ty), arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->"})`; `ax.text` adds plain text and `ax.axhline` adds a reference line.
know.why: Items ask which call draws an arrow to a peak.

know.cue: How do you colour scatter points?
know.fact: `color=` for one colour; `c=values` with `cmap="viridis"` to colour by a numeric variable (add a colorbar); `alpha=` for overlapping points; `hue=` in Seaborn for groups.
know.why: The syllabus names scatter plot colour customization.

know.cue: How do exploratory and explanatory charts differ?
know.fact: Exploratory charts are quick and many, for spotting patterns and forming hypotheses; explanatory charts are few and polished, each carrying one message for others.
know.why: The syllabus names visual exploration for hypothesis generation.

traps.cue: Why is the legend empty after `ax.legend()`?
traps.answer: The plotted series had no `label=` arguments, so there is nothing to list.

oneLine: Shape the story for the audience: executives get the answer and impact first, technical peers get method and caveats; visuals and text work as one.

know.cue: How should a presentation to executives be structured?
know.fact: Lead with the answer and recommendation (bottom line up front), show business impact with a few key numbers and simple charts, and move methodology to an appendix.
know.why: Scenario items describe an audience and ask for the best approach.

know.cue: What do technical audiences need that executives don't?
know.fact: Methods, assumptions, data sources, limitations and diagnostics, so they can judge how far to trust the result.
know.why: The contrast between audiences is the core of this objective.

know.cue: What is the structure of a data narrative?
know.fact: Context → finding → implication → recommendation, with each slide making one point stated in its title.
know.why: Items ask which slide title or sequence tells the story best.

know.cue: How should text and visuals work together?
know.fact: Text sits next to its chart and adds what the chart can't show (cause, impact, action) instead of repeating it; colours stay consistent across charts and match highlighted words.
know.why: The syllabus names harmonizing visual and textual elements.

know.cue: Which colour palette fits which data?
know.fact: Qualitative palettes for unordered groups, sequential for low-to-high values, diverging for values around a midpoint (such as correlations); choose colour-blind-safe options such as viridis.
know.why: Accessibility and palette choice are named in the syllabus.

traps.cue: Is red vs green a good way to show good vs bad?
traps.answer: Not on its own: red-green colour blindness is the most common kind. Add labels, icons or a blue-orange palette.

oneLine: Pick the findings that matter to the decision, condense them with context, and back every claim with evidence and honest limits.

know.cue: What makes a finding key?
know.fact: It is relevant to the decision, large enough to matter in practice, and reliable (enough data, consistent across checks); rank findings by impact.
know.why: Items ask which finding belongs in a short summary.

know.cue: What context does a number need?
know.fact: A comparison (previous period, target, control group), a time frame, units and a base: "churn fell from 8.1% to 6.4% in Q2", not "churn improved".
know.why: Items ask which summary statement is most informative.

know.cue: What makes evidence strong?
know.fact: It names the data source, time frame, sample size and method, shows the supporting chart or table, and states uncertainty and limitations.
know.why: The syllabus asks for articulating the basis of claims.

know.cue: What is the claim-evidence-reasoning structure?
know.fact: State the claim, present the data that supports it, explain why the data supports it, then give the recommendation that follows.
know.why: Items ask what is missing from a weak argument.

know.cue: When can you say "X causes Y"?
know.fact: When a randomized experiment (such as an A/B test) supports it; observational data only supports "X is associated with Y".
know.why: Over-claiming causation is the trap answer.

traps.answer: Without the base it may be trivial (3 units to 6). Give absolute numbers alongside percentages.

traps.cue: Is it acceptable to report only the time period where the effect was strongest?
traps.answer: No, that is cherry-picking. Report the full period, or explain why a subset is relevant.
